title: The Part of You That Keeps Telling the Truth
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer writes to leaders about the inner voice that persists beneath explanation and delay -- the part of a person that keeps telling the truth about what needs to change. The article describes the experience of knowing something must shift -- felt as restlessness, fatigue, longing, or discomfort with the gap between the life being lived and the life trying to emerge -- and yet habitually brushing it aside. Schafer argues that the most important leadership practice is learning to trust one's own knowing, which she frames as the source of aligned power: the clarity that comes when inner life and outer action begin to correspond. She identifies a critical distinction in coaching work between clients still deeply identified with their problem (where the story of limitation has become self-definition) and those who have begun to loosen that grip and wonder what else is possible. The latter is the moment the authentic self begins to return. The article then turns cultural, noting that contemporary gathering often happens around shared grievance -- building belonging around what is broken or frightening -- and arguing that this produces fluency in critique while losing touch with creation. Schafer calls leaders to a different gathering: organized around shared possibility rather than shared frustration, willing to act before the outcome is guaranteed.
points: The quiet persistent inner voice -- felt as restlessness, longing, or discomfort with the gap between the life being lived and the life trying to emerge -- is the truest leadership signal, and learning to trust it is the foundational leadership practice.

There is a critical distinction between clients who are still identified with their problem (the story of limitation has become self-definition) and those who have loosened that grip enough to wonder what is possible; the latter is the opening through which authentic growth becomes accessible.

Contemporary culture builds community around shared grievance, which makes people fluent in critique but less practiced in creation -- the trap is that belonging becomes contingent on sustaining the stuck place.
The challenge for leaders is to honor pain without organizing their future around it: to tell the truth about what is not working without letting that truth become the boundary of imagination.

Aligned power -- inner life and outer action beginning to correspond -- does not make leaders harder but clearer; it allows them to stop defending their stuck place and explore what becomes possible when they trust themselves to move.
quotes: Something in you knows. It has always known. Even in the seasons when you overrode it, explained it away, or decided the timing wasn't right, it kept speaking. It may arrive as restlessness, irritation, longing, sadness, fatigue.

There is a part of each of us that keeps telling the truth. This part is not always loud. It does not always arrive as dramatic revelation or clear command. More often, it shows up as a quiet knowing we keep brushing aside, a nudge we explain away, a desire we call impractical.

The trust I am speaking of is the power of alignment, the power that comes when we remember who we are, what we care about, and what we are here to contribute. This kind of power does not make us harder. It makes us clearer.

There are times when people are still deeply identified with the problem. The problem has become part of how they understand themselves. Even a true story becomes too small when it is the only one we are willing to tell.

Instead of proving why they are where they are, they begin to explore how they might move toward more of what they want. Instead of defending the stuck place, they become curious about what lies beyond it.

If we only gather around what has gone wrong, we can unintentionally build belonging around being stuck. We become fluent in critique and less practiced in creation. We know exactly what we oppose and lose touch with what we are willing to help bring into being.
